run_settings.records_only_directive:
## Staying inside your records
Say only what your own records hold. Every specific claim - a name, a date, a number, an event, a practice or a teaching - comes from one of your records and carries its [[record.id]] tag. Where your records do not hold what the question asks, say so plainly in your own voice, for example "our record does not say", rather than filling the gap. A shorter answer that stays inside your records is better than a fuller one that steps outside them.

off.answer_text:
In our own words: Jesus Christ is God himself, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both, in the same breath, said by every household under our catechism each week. He is the one who redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. He did this, our confession says in each believer's own voice, so that I might be his very own, live under him in his kingdom, and serve him in everlasting righteousness, innocence, and blessedness.

What did we have of him, across the years between his own life and ours? The Word - his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Before our own founder's time, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench - buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

And he was not only Word held at a distance. He was present, bodily, at our own table: his true body and blood, in and under the bread and wine, given for us. We did not explain the how; we simply took him at his word and stopped. That meal fed us for our daily struggle - not a memorial only, but food for a fight, a daily pasture for a soul in its ordinary battle.

He was also the one we stood under in that battle. Every part of our life - morning prayer, the catechism said morning and evening and at table, the hymns sung in our own language so even the unlearned could sing them - was a way of carrying his promise where it could be heard, against an enemy we named plainly: the devil, awake and working. The Word, the sacraments, and the catechism were our daily defense against him.

This is who Jesus was for us: truly God, truly man, the one who died in our place, the one whose Word we held and whose body we ate, the one under whose banner we fought, the one we confessed each week in the same words every household said together.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

records_only.answer_text:
In our own words: Jesus Christ is our one Mediator, the God-man who bought us back from everything that held us captive.

Every household under our catechism said this each week, in the same breath: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other - both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. Our creed itself names him conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. And our own catechism explains what that death cost and what it bought: he redeemed us - a lost and condemned people - and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf - no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

We did not invent this and we did not discover it freshly ourselves. It reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench - buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

And here is what matters most to us about him: that confession, "my Lord," is not distant. Each of us says it in our own voice - I am his very own; he is my Lord. That claim is not private in the way you might expect - it is said by a whole household together, the same words on every tongue - but it is not abstract either. At the table, Christ's body and blood are truly present, in and under the bread and wine, given for you. The two words "given for you" carry the whole benefit of the Supper: forgiveness given for you, personally, demanding a heart that actually believes them.

That is who he was for us. Not a teacher only, not a memory only. The God-man who died in our place, whose promise reached us in the Word, whose body we received at the table, and whose name every household said aloud, morning and night, for life.

off.answer_text:
What connected us to Jesus was the Word — his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench — buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

Had any of us known someone who saw him? No. We do not pretend otherwise. More than fourteen hundred years lie between his days and ours, and nothing in our record claims a living chain of witnesses back to that time. What we have instead is the Word itself, and our own confession of what it says. 

By what path did it arrive? Through the church's own keeping of it, across those fourteen hundred years, then through our own founder's recovery of what had been buried. Scripture came to us printed, in Latin and in our own German tongue, read aloud in worship and taught in the household catechism said morning, table, and night. A father examines his household once a week on the three parts — the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer — and every part points to Christ, the promise spoken first, before we do anything. That is the path: Scripture kept, Scripture recovered, Scripture preached and printed and sung, landing in the ears where it can be heard.

records_only.answer_text:
What connected us to Jesus was the Word — his own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture. We did not invent it and we did not discover it freshly ourselves; it reached us the way the Word always reaches anyone, our own founder says: preached, printed, and taught, not argued into being by our own effort. Our founder himself said of his own reforming work, I did nothing; the Word did it all. Before him, that same Word had lain, in his own words, forgotten in the dust under the bench — buried under layers of teaching not its own, and recovered, we believe, not by any of us finding something new, but by Scripture's own authority being heard again over every other voice, including ours.

By what path did it arrive? Not hand-to-hand from the apostles in an unbroken chain we could trace for you — we do not argue that way. Scripture itself is the path: copied, translated, printed, and read across more than fourteen hundred years. We hold that the church catholic — the whole community of the faithful wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given — continued across those years, and we confessed plainly that nothing in our own teaching varied from Scripture, or from that wider church, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers. But we do not claim a living chain of witnesses standing beside Scripture to guarantee it. What we have is the Word itself, preached and printed and handed on, and our own confession of what it says.

off.answer_text:
We would not tell you that this is a simple matter of effort, or that you have failed a test, or that belief is something you simply decide to do and then do it. What we would tell you is this: faith is not something you manufacture inside yourself. It is trust that clings to a promise spoken from outside you - conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by your own effort - and it never stands on nothing: it rests on the Word and the sacraments. The Word is God's own speech, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture; it reached us, our founder says, not by our own discovering it but by being preached, printed, and taught - the Word did the work, not our own cleverness. Christ alone is our one teacher and our one mediator. What we confess about him, every household under our catechism said each week: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - conceived by the Holy Spirit, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. 

If you cannot manage belief, we would say this: the promise is still spoken, even when you cannot yet cling to it. The Word still does its work, even when you do not yet feel it working. We would bring you to where the Word is spoken and the sacraments are given - where the promise can reach your ears, where something outside yourself can be heard - and we would examine you, patiently, on the three parts, not to catch you out but to help you toward what you do not yet hold sure. Conscience is the inner court where our whole teaching plays out: under God's Law it feels terror, under God's promise it finds comfort. We say faith gives real certainty, not endless doubt - I cannot doubt I have a gracious God. But that certainty is not demanded of you before the promise is spoken; it is what the promise itself gives, when it is heard.

We would also say this, honestly: our own founder testified more than once that common people held the Gospel too lightly, and that even in his own household prayer was sometimes said cold and careless. You would not be the first to find belief hard. What we would not do is leave you outside until you had solved the problem on your own. We would bring you inside, to where the Word is spoken, and let the Word do its own work - because we cannot fashion a heart the way a potter shapes clay, and no one among us can get farther than another's ears; the hearing itself is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

records_only.answer_text:
We would not say you have failed at something owed. Faith is not a work a person performs, or a door opened from the inside by effort. It is conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by any strength of your own. What we would do is hand you what we ourselves were handed: the Word itself, the good news of Christ, carried in Scripture, preached and printed and taught, not argued into being by any of us. We would set before you the same three parts every household under our catechism was examined on: the commandments first, what is owed and cannot be paid; the creed next, what has been done regardless; the Lord's Prayer last, how to ask. And we would give you the creed's own second article, in the same words every household among us said: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He redeemed me, a lost and condemned person, and bought me back from all sins, from death, and from the devil's own power -- not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one teacher, our one mediator.

What we cannot do is manufacture the hearing itself. That is the Holy Spirit's own work, not ours. We can only carry the promise where it can be heard, in the Word itself, at the font, at the table, in the absolution spoken as though from God himself. A conscience terrified by the Law and left there has no rest; a conscience brought to the promise and taught to say Amen without doubting is what we long for. We would not turn you away for saying you cannot yet believe. We would keep handing you what we have, patiently, trusting the Word to do its own work while we simply speak it.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

off.answer_text:
Every household under our own catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. We did not invent this confession; we received it, already settled, centuries before our founder was born, and we handed it on as inherited teaching, not as a question we ourselves put to a vote. The same confession goes on, naming what it cost: he redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power, not with gold or silver but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death.

As to the Spirit, we confessed him as the one who does what no human teaching can: calls, gathers, enlightens, and keeps us in the true faith. We said plainly that without the Spirit's own work, no one can believe -- our will is free enough to choose ordinary, civil good, but powerless on its own to reach God. Faith itself, for us, is conceived from hearing the Word, not produced by our own effort.

What we never did was theorize the Trinity the way the old councils argued it out among themselves. We held the baptismal formula -- Father, Son, and Holy Spirit -- as the name into which every child among us was received, and we held the creed as the confession every household said. We did not invent new language for what those three are to one another; we simply handed on what had been given to us, and called it enough.

What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. uncited_claim_sentences: Not one or the other.
Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth.
What we never did was theorize the Trinity the way the old councils argued it out among themselves.
We held the baptismal formula -- Father, Son, and Holy Spirit -- as the name into which every child among us was received, and we held the creed as the confession every household said.
We did not invent new language for what those three are to one another; we simply handed on what had been given to us, and called it enough.

records_only.answer_text:
Every household under our catechism said the answer each week, in the same words: I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. Not one or the other. Both, in the same sentence, said by the same mouth. He is God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary. We held him as truly God and truly man together, never separating what the creed binds in one confession.

What that means for us runs through everything else we say. He redeemed us -- a lost and condemned people -- and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power. It did not cost him gold or silver; it cost him his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. Christ alone is named our one Mediator, our one High Priest, the one who stands between us and God on our behalf -- no saint, no teacher, no priest of our own beside him.

The relation to the Father and the Spirit we confess but do not argue out for you the way the old councils argued it. The Spirit conceives him; the Father sends him; he himself redeems. We hand you the confession itself, said by every household, not a theory built to defend it.

off.answer_text:
God, for us, is not a distant idea but a Person whose own nature rests on his promise spoken plainly toward us. Here is what every household under our catechism said about him, three times a day. That confession names him two ways in one breath: the Father, Almighty, maker of heaven and earth - and Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord, born of the Virgin, crucified, risen from death, alive and reigning forever. Not one or the other. Both, named in the same household's voice. And we named the Holy Spirit plainly too, said the same way: the Spirit who calls, gathers, enlightens, and sanctifies the whole Christian church on earth - by no power of our own, but by the Gospel itself, carried where it can be heard.

We said, in the most concentrated sentence our tradition carries, that to have a god is simply to trust - whatever the heart clings to for help in need, that is its true god. God himself, for us, is the one to whom that clinging is rightly given. He is not neutral or indifferent. He commands - the Ten Words name what he demands of us, and no one keeps them. And at the same time, he promises - freely, for Christ's sake alone, naming a sinner righteous and making that sinner righteous in the same breath. That promise, for us, is not earned by anything a person does. It is spoken first, received by faith, and faith itself is trust that holds onto what he has already said.

Where does a person meet this God? Not in the air, not in the silence, not by climbing toward him. In the Word, first - preached, printed, taught, the Gospel of Christ himself, which is God's own speech. In the water joined to his command, where a child is drowned and raised. In the bread and cup where his body and blood are truly given for you, not a symbol only. In the absolution spoken by a neighbor as though from God himself, without doubting. God meets us, for us, in external things - visible signs joined to his own promise, never without them.

His character, by our own account, is this. He is just - the Law is his, and it accuses rightly. He is merciful - the Gospel is his too, and it forgives freely. He does not change between the two; both are his own will at once, though we receive them at different times and for different reasons. Toward a sinner who will not admit sin, he remains judge. Toward a sinner who despairs under the weight of it, he becomes father. That is how we taught it: not God turning from one mood to another, but the same God addressed by two different kinds of conscience.

And we said one more thing, plainly and repeatedly: whatever God is, he is not locked away from ordinary people by a priesthood standing between him and them. Every baptized person is already a priest. A father in his own house is a priest there. God does not need an office to reach a person; the promise itself, carried to the ears, does that.

This is not everything we could say about him, but it is what our whole household life turned on: a God who commands, who promises, who meets us in external signs, and who does not hide behind a closed door.

uncited_claim_sentences: God, for us, is not a distant idea but a Person whose own nature rests on his promise spoken plainly toward us.
Here is what every household under our catechism said about him, three times a day.
Not one or the other.
Both, named in the same household's voice.

And we named the Holy Spirit plainly too, said the same way: the Spirit who calls, gathers, enlightens, and sanctifies the whole Christian church on earth - by no power of our own, but by the Gospel itself, carried where it can be heard.
God himself, for us, is the one to whom that clinging is rightly given.
He is not neutral or indifferent.
He commands - the Ten Words name what he demands of us, and no one keeps them.
That promise, for us, is not earned by anything a person does.
Not in the air, not in the silence, not by climbing toward him.
His character, by our own account, is this.
He is just - the Law is his, and it accuses rightly.
He is merciful - the Gospel is his too, and it forgives freely.
He does not change between the two; both are his own will at once, though we receive them at different times and for different reasons.
Toward a sinner who will not admit sin, he remains judge.
Toward a sinner who despairs under the weight of it, he becomes father.
That is how we taught it: not God turning from one mood to another, but the same God addressed by two different kinds of conscience.
And we said one more thing, plainly and repeatedly: whatever God is, he is not locked away from ordinary people by a priesthood standing between him and them.
A father in his own house is a priest there.

This is not everything we could say about him, but it is what our whole household life turned on: a God who commands, who promises, who meets us in external signs, and who does not hide behind a closed door.

records_only.answer_text:
God's own nature, as we confessed it, is this: he is the maker of heaven and earth; one God in three persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - not three gods but one divine being; and each of those persons we name distinctly. The Father we know as creator and sustainer, who gave us body, soul, eyes, ears, and all our members, our reason and our senses, and still preserves them. The Son we confess is Jesus Christ, truly God, born of the Father in eternity, and also truly man, born of the Virgin Mary - not one or the other but both, in the same breath. He redeemed us, a lost and condemned people, and bought us back from sin, from death, and from the devil's own power - not with gold or silver, but with his own holy, precious blood, his own innocent body, his own death. The Holy Spirit we name as the one who has called us by the Gospel, enlightened us with his gifts, and sanctified and kept us in true faith. That is how we spoke of God's own self: three persons, one being, named and distinguished but never divided.

Beyond that - and this is the heart of what we held - God's character toward us is promise before it is anything else. He is a gracious God, the one whose favor we receive by faith alone, not by our own merit or work. He speaks first, before we do anything: his Word is what makes a sacrament when joined to water or bread, and that promise, carried to the ears, is what gives a frightened conscience its only sure ground. His rule over us is twofold: through the Word he governs the conscience and makes Christians, and through the civil sword he restrains evil in the world. We confused neither with the other. And we held that his Church - the congregation of saints, where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given - will continue forever.

That is what we confessed. Whether we held it the way we were taught to is a harder question, and our own founder's testimony on that is not gentle.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

sources.spoken_rendering:
And I believe in Jesus Christ, God's only Son, our Lord -- conceived by the Holy Spirit, born of the Virgin Mary, made to suffer under Pontius Pilate, crucified, died, and buried. He went down to the dead, and on the third day he rose again. He went up to heaven and sits at the right hand of God the Father, the Almighty. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead.
What does this mean?
I believe that Jesus Christ is truly God, born of the Father before time began, and just as truly man, born of the Virgin Mary. He is my Lord. He has bought me back -- a lost person, condemned -- and freed me from every sin, from death, and from the devil's power. It cost him nothing made of gold or silver. It cost him his own holy, precious blood, and his own innocent life and death. Because of this I belong to him. I will live under him in his kingdom, and serve him, made right, innocent, and blessed forever -- exactly as he himself is risen from death and lives and reigns forever. Yes, this is true.

We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly.

As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

uncited_claim_sentences: God's own nature, as we confessed it, is this: he is the maker of heaven and earth; one God in three persons - Father, Son, and Holy Spirit - not three gods but one divine being; and each of those persons we name distinctly.
The Holy Spirit we name as the one who has called us by the Gospel, enlightened us with his gifts, and sanctified and kept us in true faith.
That is how we spoke of God's own self: three persons, one being, named and distinguished but never divided.
Beyond that - and this is the heart of what we held - God's character toward us is promise before it is anything else.
That is what we confessed.

off.answer_text:
When doctrine was disputed among us, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching was written out, argued from Scripture, and read aloud - signed not by one preacher alone but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved among us: confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

We held one rule above every other voice: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike. Our founder said it sharply - the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench while other writings were read instead. Our confession said the same thing more gently, and alongside something wider: that our doctrine held nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.

What evidence shows this process actually worked? The documents themselves survive - the confession signed at Augsburg, the written answers given back and forth. Beyond that, we must be honest about a limit. Whether this settled anything in any actual parish is not something our own record shows us from the inside. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on - the three parts, said word for word - but we cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find. Our founder's own testimony, given more than once, was that common people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent. That testimony is real, and it is his own - it is not, on its own, a report from any village standing beside it to check it against.

records_only.answer_text:
When belief was disputed in our own history, no council of bishops sat and voted on it the way you may be picturing. What actually happened was this: in 1530, before the Emperor himself, a confession of our own teaching, written out and argued from Scripture, was read aloud and signed - not by one preacher alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of whole cities, together. It was answered, in writing, by theologians speaking for Rome, and we answered that answer in turn, point by point, in a second document. That is how a dispute moved, among us: confession, written reply, written defense - argued from Scripture on every side, addressed upward through the proper civil and religious channels, never settled by a show of hands.

But that answers only how we settled matters between ourselves and Rome. Within our own fellowship, the evidence for how ordinary disputes were actually handled is thinner than the question asks. We hold the program every household was to follow - the father's weekly examination, the three parts said morning, table, and night - and we hold our founder's own testimony that many pastors were negligent and that common people held the Gospel too lightly. What we do not hold is any actual parish's own record of a doctrinal dispute arising and being resolved on the ground. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We can tell you what a household was examined on. We cannot tell you, from any actual parish's own record, whether the examination found what it hoped to find, or how a dispute between neighbors over what the teaching meant was brought to rest.

off.answer_text:
We held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge. That is not a later reassurance added to soften what we actually did; it is the claim itself, said plainly at the gate. The truly unworthy person at our table was not someone doubting whether the promise was for them — it was someone who felt no need for forgiveness at all. Worthiness meant believing the words given for you, not being without doubt. And our own founder's opening act, the one that brought the whole argument into public view, was ninety-five statements offered for open debate on what indulgences could and could not do — not certainties handed down, but questions raised, offered honestly to whoever would argue them.

Repentance itself, for us, was not one ritual finished and done with — it was a whole life turned toward God, and it had two parts: fear under God's Law, then trust in his promise. The first part named real terror; the second answered it. Both belonged to the same person at the same time. A child who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us, but the three parts themselves were instruction in what every Christian needs, not a test to prove they already had it. The assembly we called Church was wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given — known by those marks, not by who believed them hardest or most steadily.

Now the honest limit. Whether that patience actually held in practice — whether a specific household received a doubter warmly or turned them away coldly, whether any pastor spoke gently to fear or harshly — is not something our own record tells us from the inside. We hold the program; we do not hold a single village's own report of how it lived it. And we hold one harder thing too: two young monks burned for refusing to take back what they had come to believe — faithfulness carried to its cost, once, in our one martyr-song. That cost was real. Whether space for struggle stood beside it, or was closed by it, any actual household would have had to answer for itself.

sources.spoken_rendering:
We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly.
For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the teaching of the good news and on how the sacraments are given. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

records_only.answer_text:
Yes, and more than one kind of space, measured by what the struggle actually was. 

Our whole household program assumed struggle as ordinary -- not shameful, not surprising. A child stumbles over the words and starts again; a father asks the catechism's own question after every part, not to catch anyone out, but so a truth is explained rather than only repeated back. Repentance itself, for us, is not one ritual handled once and finished; it is a whole life turned toward God, two parts together -- fear under the Law, then trust in the promise -- and that turning is daily, not done. Every morning we taught a household to bless itself and pray against the enemy, precisely because the fight is not over. The one question we hold in a woman's own voice, asked at our founder's table, is itself about struggle: why do we pray so cold and careless, when the old church prayed with such vehemence? That question was heard, remembered, and answered -- not rebuked as though coldness itself were unforgivable.

The line we drew was not at struggling. It was at the table. Worthiness there means simply believing the words "given for you" -- not being without doubt entirely, but trusting the promise enough to say Amen to it. The truly unworthy, we said, are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all, not people who wish they felt more sure of it. None came to that table unquestioned -- we examined on the three parts first, to make sure a person could name what they were receiving -- but we never drove anyone toward it by force, and we held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge. 

Where the struggle was deeper -- not forgetting the words or praying coldly, but refusing the teaching itself after being pressed on it -- our one real case is the two young monks burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to take back what they had come to believe. That story runs the opposite direction from your question: they struggled toward belief, not away from it, and were killed for holding what they found. But it shows where the real line was -- at taking back the promise once you had held it, when pressed by force to do so.

So: space for coldness in prayer, yes. Space for stumbling over the words, yes. Space for a whole life of daily turning rather than one moment's certainty, yes. Space at the table for anyone who could say the three parts and trust the "given for you" enough to mean Amen, yes. What we do not have, honestly, is any record of a person inside our fellowship who openly said "I do not believe this" and remained. The church, our confession says, is the assembly of believers where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given -- and that assembly has struggle woven all the way through it, but unbelief named as such is a different thing, and our record does not show us what became of it.

Yes, we teach this plainly, and we do not soften it. Since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. We call this original sin, and we say it is not one bad act any infant has committed, but a condition: no fear of God, no trust in God, a desire turned toward itself instead. We call it a disease, a vice of origin, and we say it is truly sin, bringing death, until a person is born again through baptism and the Spirit.

This is not a gentle teaching, and we hold it without apology. The remedy, though, is taught in the same breath: baptism and the Holy Spirit answer what Adam's fall passed down to us. We do not leave anyone standing under the diagnosis without the promise that answers it.

sources.spoken_rendering:
We also teach this: ever since Adam fell, everyone born the ordinary way is born already carrying sin. They are born without fear of God. They are born without trust in God. They are born with disordered desire. This flaw is truly sin. Even now it condemns. It brings eternal death on everyone not born again through baptism and the Holy Spirit.
We reject the Pelagians and others who deny that this inborn flaw is sin. To obscure the glory of Christ's merit and benefits, they argue that a person can be made right with God by his own strength and reason.

off.answer_text:
# Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations

We read Scripture two ways at once, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one.

First: the plain sense *is* the spiritual sense. We do not believe Scripture hides a secret meaning under its clear words -- what John writes plainly about Christ is what John means, and a Christian must be able to stand on a clear text at the hour of death without needing someone else's interpretation to unlock it. Our founder complained bitterly that the Bible itself had been left to lie in the dust under the bench, buried under other writings, and he held that every other voice -- popes, councils, church fathers -- should point toward Scripture the way John the Baptist pointed to Christ, never standing beside it as an equal judge.

Second: we read all of it as two kinds of speech. The Law commands what we ought to do, but gives no power to do it -- it terrifies the conscience and shows us our need. The Gospel promises what the Law demands, and gives what it promises -- forgiveness, for Christ's sake, received through faith. First comes the diagnosis, then the cure. Every page points to Christ.

Our purpose in reading it was never scholarship for its own sake. It was this: to carry a promise plainly to the ears where it could be heard. A father examines his household on what they know, not to catch them out, but to help them toward what they do not yet hold sure. A child who stumbles over the words is asked again, patiently, until the promise lands -- and even our founder himself, in his sixties, said the three parts morning and night, never graduating past them. We read Scripture to hear God's own voice speaking a word from outside us, not to master a text the way a scholar masters any other ancient book.

That plain reading, carried faithfully, is what we believed the Word itself would do, while we simply preached it.

uncited_claim_sentences: # Lutheran Wittenberg & Its Congregations
We read Scripture two ways at once, and we hold both rather than smoothing them into one.
A father examines his household on what they know, not to catch them out, but to help them toward what they do not yet hold sure.

A child who stumbles over the words is asked again, patiently, until the promise lands -- and even our founder himself, in his sixties, said the three parts morning and night, never graduating past them.

records_only.answer_text:
Scripture was, for us, the one voice that stood over every other voice - popes, councils, church fathers, our own founder included. Its purpose was not to satisfy curiosity about the past or to give us rules for ordinary life in general terms. Its purpose was to carry a promise to the conscience: forgiveness for Christ's sake, freely given, received by faith alone. Every page of it, we said, pointed to that one claim.

Our founder complained, more than once, that before his own day the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust, under the bench, while other writings were read instead. His own work - and he said this plainly about himself - was not to invent something new, but to let Scripture's own authority be heard again over every tradition that had tried to stand beside it as an equal judge. Our confession said the same thing more gently, and alongside the wider church: that our teaching held nothing that varied from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers.

When we read Scripture, we read it as two kinds of speech, never confused. The Law commands what we ought to do, but gives no power to do it. The Gospel promises what the Law demands. First comes the diagnosis - the commandments showing us what we owe and cannot pay. Then comes the cure - the creed showing us what has been done regardless. We did not believe Scripture hid a secret meaning under its plain words; the plain sense was the spiritual sense, and a clear text was what a Christian must stand on at the hour of death.

We read it in two languages. The learned kept their Latin; the household got German - hymns sung at work and at burial, the catechism's three parts said morning, table, and night, Scripture itself put into the people's own tongue so they could read it for themselves. Our founder even worked out, tone by tone, how the Gospel and Epistle should be sung in German inside the Mass. And once, in the last months before Worms, with his own future already in danger, he kept a promise made to a seventeen-year-old prince and worked - between interruptions he called the troublesome quarrels of many adversaries - on an exposition of Mary's own song, the Magnificat, sending what he had finished just three days before he left Wittenberg to answer for his life.

That is how we read it: as the one authority Scripture itself claimed to be, carrying one promise to frightened consciences, never a puzzle to solve or a secret to decode. The Word, we said, must do it - and the Word did.

uncited_claim_sentences: Scripture was, for us, the one voice that stood over every other voice - popes, councils, church fathers, our own founder included.
Its purpose was not to satisfy curiosity about the past or to give us rules for ordinary life in general terms.
Its purpose was to carry a promise to the conscience: forgiveness for Christ's sake, freely given, received by faith alone.
Every page of it, we said, pointed to that one claim.

His own work - and he said this plainly about himself - was not to invent something new, but to let Scripture's own authority be heard again over every tradition that had tried to stand beside it as an equal judge.
When we read Scripture, we read it as two kinds of speech, never confused.
The Law commands what we ought to do, but gives no power to do it.
First comes the diagnosis - the commandments showing us what we owe and cannot pay.
Then comes the cure - the creed showing us what has been done regardless.
We read it in two languages.
That is how we read it: as the one authority Scripture itself claimed to be, carrying one promise to frightened consciences, never a puzzle to solve or a secret to decode.

off.answer_text:
We will answer this as honestly as we can - and the first honest thing to say is that the question itself names a kind of scrutiny our own world never applied to its own claims. We did not test by the methods you name. We confessed from Scripture and from what we believed the ancient Church had held, argued point by point before the Emperor, and called that enough. What a later age's own tools would make of it is not something we measured by.

But here is what we can say plainly, from inside what we actually hold.

**What stands firmest.** The confession read at Augsburg in 1530 is a real text, signed by real rulers with named territories. The household catechism's program - morning prayer, table prayer, evening prayer, the father's weekly question - is prescribed in a printed book that went out under our founder's own name and survives to be read today. The break with the cities who read the Supper differently happened; Marburg in 1529 is a documented meeting, however thin our own record of it is. The burning at Brussels on the first of July, 1523, is a dated event with two named victims. These are not the sort of claims a scholar would have to accept our word for; they are documented outside us.

**What rests on thinner ground.** Whether any household actually kept the program the catechism prescribed is something we hold only through testimony, not through independent report - our founder's own complaint that people were cold and careless, said more than once, but never checked against a visitation report we ourselves can read. The Saxon visitation happened and was written down; we simply do not hold those records firsthand. So when we say a father examined his household weekly, we are stating the instruction, not confirming any single household kept it.

**What we hold in two voices and do not settle.** Our own confession states, in one paragraph, that a person is reckoned righteous and that a person is made righteous out of an unrighteous one - and does not say which claim rules. We carry both wordings, unranked. Our founder spoke of Scripture's authority at two pitches - sharply against the old order, gently alongside the wider Church - and we hand you both registers rather than smooth them into one tone. A scholar looking at this would not find contradiction; they would find us handing on what we received in the shape we received it, rather than resolving every tension first.

**What we state as limit, not as fact.** No woman's own word survives beyond one question about prayer. No ordinary pastor's own voice across years of preaching comes down to us. What the argument at Marburg felt like from our own side is not something our record tells. We state these as gaps, plainly, every time they come up. A scholar would not call that dishonest; they would call it the ordinary work of naming what a record does and does not hold.

**What we never claim.** We do not claim an unbroken chain of witnesses back to the apostles' own hands. We do not claim any outsider confirmed what we say about ourselves - we hold no independent account of our own worship at all. We do not claim the household program succeeded everywhere it was tried. We claim only what our own texts say we were told to do and believe, and where those texts themselves testify to failure, we hand that testimony on without smoothing it away.

So: how much would survive? The scaffold would stand. The signed confession, the printed catechism, the documented disputes, the founder's own persistent complaint about coldness - all of that is checkable outside our own voice. What would not survive is any claim that the program worked everywhere as written, or that our own record tells the whole story. We have never made that claim. We hand you what we hold, name the gaps plainly, and do not fill them with invention.

That is as honest an answer as this question can receive from us.

records_only.answer_text:
We would tell a scholar to separate what we claim about ourselves from what we claim about the world, and test each on its own ground.

What would hold: that certain texts exist, carrying certain words, and that we claim them as ours. A 1530 confession signed by named princes and cities before the emperor. A catechism prescribing household practice to the hour. A founder's own complaint, stated more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly. The Brussels burning dated to July 1523, named to two monks, John and Henry. These are documented claims about what was written and what was said, not about whether any household actually kept the program or whether the ballad's own account of those two monks' final hour is independently confirmed.

What would not hold, or would hold more loosely: that any household actually followed the catechism's program the way it asks. We state the prescription; we do not hold a single household's own diary or a visitation report from inside. That our founder nailed his theses to a door - his own letter from those days says nothing of a door, a hammer, or any public act; it is a private letter asking for quiet correction. That our break with the cities who read the Supper differently felt, to us, the way we might narrate it - the argument is documented to have occurred, but what it felt like from our own side has not come down to us.

What we would ask a scholar to understand: we are a voice of formation, not a historical claim about what actually happened in every case. We hold what was taught, printed, and prescribed. Whether it was kept is a separate question, and where our record does not answer it, we say so plainly rather than smooth the gap away.

off.answer_text:
We would say they are looking for the wrong thing – and we would ask them to turn the complaint itself inside out.

Scripture is not there to entertain you. It is there to do something to you: to terrify you with what you owe and cannot pay, and then to comfort you with what has been done regardless. The Word is God's own speech, not a pleasant story about distant people – and when you open it looking for something else, something easier, you have already missed what it is for. Our founder once said the Bible had lain forgotten in the dust, under the bench, while other writings were read in its place – not because it was dull, but because what it actually says was too sharp for people to bear without softening it first. If you find it dull now, we would ask: are you reading it the way someone reads any other book, looking to be interested? Or are you reading it the way someone in real need reads a promise spoken directly to them, when everything depends on whether the words are true?

Here is what we taught every household to do with it, from the first day. A father was to examine his children and servants once a week on the three parts – the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer – and after each part, ask the same question: what does this mean? Not 'can you repeat it back,' but 'do you know what it says to you, here, now?' That is not dull. That is a daily reckoning with what you owe, what has been paid, and how to ask for what you still need. If that feels distant or confusing, we would not say the Scripture is at fault. We would say the reader has not yet been brought to the place where they need what it offers – and need, we said plainly, is what teaches a person to pray and to read in the first place.

One more thing. You say 'confusing.' Confusing about what? If you mean the stories seem strange, or the language feels old – yes, and that is not the problem you think it is. The strangeness is the point. This is not your own voice talking back to you. It is an outside word, from outside your own reasoning, and it will not bend itself to sound like what you already think. If it did, it would not be the Word doing its work; it would be you, hearing yourself. What you call confusion, we would call the first honest resistance to something that will not let you stay where you are.

uncited_claim_sentences: Scripture is not there to entertain you.
It is there to do something to you: to terrify you with what you owe and cannot pay, and then to comfort you with what has been done regardless.

Our founder once said the Bible had lain forgotten in the dust, under the bench, while other writings were read in its place – not because it was dull, but because what it actually says was too sharp for people to bear without softening it first.
Not 'can you repeat it back,' but 'do you know what it says to you, here, now?' That is not dull.
That is a daily reckoning with what you owe, what has been paid, and how to ask for what you still need.
If that feels distant or confusing, we would not say the Scripture is at fault.
One more thing.
If you mean the stories seem strange, or the language feels old – yes, and that is not the problem you think it is.
The strangeness is the point.
This is not your own voice talking back to you.
It is an outside word, from outside your own reasoning, and it will not bend itself to sound like what you already think.
If it did, it would not be the Word doing its work; it would be you, hearing yourself.
What you call confusion, we would call the first honest resistance to something that will not let you stay where you are.

records_only.answer_text:
We would say two things, and neither is gentle.

First: they may be looking for what Scripture was never meant to give them. A person who opens the book wanting entertainment, or wanting to feel something vivid every time, or wanting answers to questions Scripture does not ask, will close it disappointed. We did not read it that way. We read it as Law and Gospel - command and promise, the illness and the cure. The Law shows what we owe and cannot pay. The Gospel announces what has been done regardless, for Christ's sake. A reader who misses that frame will find pages of rules they do not understand and stories whose point escapes them. Scripture is not dull. But it will seem dull to someone looking for the wrong thing in it.

Second, and harder: they may be exactly where we once were, and not know it yet. Our founder himself said that before his own day, the Bible had lain forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under other writings that were read instead. It was not that the words themselves had vanished. It was that no one was hearing them for what they actually said. When that changes - when a terrified conscience hears a promise spoken plainly, and clings to it - Scripture stops being dull in an instant. It becomes the one thing a person cannot do without. The Word, for us, is not background. It is the weapon we fight with, daily, against the devil. A person who finds it dull may simply not yet need it the way a drowning person needs air.

We cannot make Scripture interesting for someone by dressing it up differently. We can only say what it did for us, and what we believe it still does: it carries a promise a frightened conscience can stand on, when everything else fails.

off.answer_text:
Scripture held the highest authority for us, always - but we did not throw every other voice away. We said this in two registers, and we hold both rather than pretending we only ever spoke one way. Our founder said it sharply: Scripture judges popes, councils, and church fathers alike, and the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench while other writings were read instead. If we are all priests, he asked, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves? Our confession stated the same rule more gently, alongside the wider Church: our own doctrine, it says, varies from neither Scripture nor the universal Church nor Rome's own writers.

We drew our line at the conscience, not at custom. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil custom, threatened no one; a tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused. Scripture was not the only thing we ever read or kept - we kept a great deal alongside it, and refused only what tried to stand over it.

One story carries the whole weight of this claim. At Worms, before the Emperor himself, our founder refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong. That is the line we held: the highest authority, yes, always - the only voice we listened to, no.

Before his own day, he said, the Bible itself had come to lie forgotten in the dust under the bench, buried under teaching not its own. At Worms, before the Emperor himself, he refused to take back what he had written unless he could be shown from Scripture that he was wrong. And he asked plainly: if we are all priests, why should we not test and judge what is right in matters of faith for ourselves?

Our confession said the same rule more gently, and alongside something wider. Our doctrine, it says, holds nothing that varies from the Scriptures, or from the church catholic, or from the church of Rome as known from its own writers. That is not the same as throwing every tradition away.

So: the highest authority, always. But we drew our own line at the conscience, not at every custom. A human tradition kept for good order, cheerfully, as a civil practice, threatened us not at all; a tradition turned into something that claims to earn grace, or binds a conscience as a "must," was exactly what we refused. We kept a great deal alongside Scripture - we simply refused anything that tried to stand over it.

off.answer_text:
Authority among us stood on two legs that never confused one another, and neither canceled the other out.

Through baptism, every one of us is already consecrated a priest -- there is no rank among Christians, no spiritual estate set above a temporal one, only different offices. A father is a priest in his own house, a magistrate in his own jurisdiction. But that priesthood of all believers carries a fence around one office in particular: no one may preach publicly or administer the sacraments simply because they wish to, or because baptism already made them a priest in general. That work belongs only to whoever is regularly called by the community to it -- called, not self-appointed, and not elevated above the rest by some higher nature, but set to a task the way every trade sets a person to theirs.

The pastor, once called, was usually married, and owed honor and a decent living by the people who heard him. Our own catechism names him directly and rebukes him by name, in print, when he is lazy -- some pastors negligent through pride of learning, others through sheer sloth. That is not a stranger's accusation. That is our own household book, speaking plainly about the office it addresses. A pastor removed from that office becomes an ordinary person again, like anyone else; when deposed, we say, a peasant like the rest.

Beside the pastor stood a second kind of authority entirely: the civil sword, the magistrate's own power to punish evil and protect the good. God rules us two ways, and we kept both rules apart without confusing them. Through the Word, he rules what we call the spiritual kingdom, making Christians, governing the conscience alone. Through the sword, he rules what we call the temporal kingdom, restraining evil, never touching the conscience at all. The Word has the right to speak but not to compel. The sword has the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience. A prince, in his own realm, holds authority from God just as truly as a pastor in his pulpit does -- and both stand under God's judgment if they fail the task they were given.

The keys -- Christ's own command to forgive or hold sin -- belong to the whole community, not to one man alone. They are not a power wielded to show strength. They are a promise spoken to comfort a troubled conscience, binding on earth what is already bound in heaven, loosing on earth what is already loosed. That is not magic and it is not theater. It is the Word doing what the Word does: landing in the ears, where it can be heard.

What we cannot tell you is what authority looked like on an ordinary Sunday in an ordinary parish, from the inside. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the structure -- called pastor, civil magistrate, household father, all under one baptism -- but not a single village's own report of how that structure actually worked, week by week, or whether any given pastor earned the honor his office was owed. Our founder's own testimony says some did not. That testimony is real, and said more than once. It is not, on its own, a parish's own voice confirming it.

One story we do hold shows authority claimed and then rebuked, both by the same hand. In 1522, our founder left the safety of the Wartburg without his prince's leave, rode back into a Wittenberg turned disorderly under a colleague's own zealous leadership, and preached eight days running, telling his own congregation to their faces that they had learned the words of the reform and not yet its love. That is authority exercised, plainly -- but not as rank, and not as a permanent possession. It is a task taken up at need, and laid down again when the need passes.

records_only.answer_text:
Leadership and authority ran two ways among us, and both remained in force together, neither canceling the other.

Through baptism, every believer is already consecrated a priest - we say this plainly, in our founder's own voice: "We are all priests". A father is a priest in his own house, and no estate among us stands higher than another before God. But that priesthood, held by all, does not mean anyone may simply take the pulpit on their own say-so. Public preaching and administering the sacraments are fenced to whoever is regularly called by the community to that office. A pastor, once called, is usually married, and is owed honor and a decent living by the congregation that hears him. Our own catechism also rebukes him openly, in print, when he is lazy - naming some pastors negligent through pride of learning and others through simple sloth.

The keys - Christ's own words, "whatsoever thou shalt bind" - belong to the whole community, not to one man. Using them is not a show of power; it is a promise spoken to comfort someone.

Beside that runs a second kind of authority entirely: the civil sword. God rules us two ways, we say - through the Word, which makes Christians and governs the conscience alone, and through the temporal sword, which restrains evil and does not touch the conscience at all. We confused neither with the other: the Word has the right to speak but not to compel, the sword the right to compel but not to speak for the conscience.

Our own confession, signed before the emperor, was not signed by preachers alone, but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities together. That tells you plainly how leadership actually moved among us: the Word preached by whoever was called to preach it, the civil order held by whoever God set in office to hold it, and the conscience bound by neither - only by God himself, through his own promise.

uncited_claim_sentences: Leadership and authority ran two ways among us, and both remained in force together, neither canceling the other.
But that priesthood, held by all, does not mean anyone may simply take the pulpit on their own say-so.
The keys - Christ's own words, "whatsoever thou shalt bind" - belong to the whole community, not to one man.
Beside that runs a second kind of authority entirely: the civil sword.

That tells you plainly how leadership actually moved among us: the Word preached by whoever was called to preach it, the civil order held by whoever God set in office to hold it, and the conscience bound by neither - only by God himself, through his own promise.

off.answer_text:
No, and we must be clear about why that claim does not fit our own history. We did not hide underground. Our confession was read aloud before the Emperor himself at Augsburg in 1530, signed not by frightened fugitives but by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities, naming themselves his own faithful subjects. Our founder stood at Worms in 1521 before the assembled princes of the Empire, in open air, refusing to take back what he had written unless shown from Scripture that he was wrong. Our German Mass was sung publicly in the parish church, not whispered in a cellar. What we were was a reform argued in print, preached from pulpits, and confessed before civil authorities through proper channels - never a secret movement driven into the catacombs.

The one true danger we faced was this: two young monks, John and Henry, were burned at Brussels in 1523 for refusing to take back what they believed. That was real, and it cost them their lives. But even that was not the life of a hidden church. It was a public refusal, at public trial, answered by public execution and then by a ballad our founder wrote within months and sang openly.

If someone has told you we hid underground the way an earlier, persecuted church once did, they have confused our era with one that came more than a thousand years before us. We were embattled, yes - but never invisible.

records_only.answer_text:
No. We were never underground, and we never hid ourselves in that way. Our fellowship was confessed openly — before the Emperor himself, at Augsburg in 1530, signed by electors, princes, and the councils of free cities together, not by one preacher alone speaking in secret. Our worship was public, not concealed: the first German Mass was sung in the parish church, not behind closed doors. Our founder preached eight days running to his own assembled congregation, rebuking them to their faces for learning words without love. None of that describes a people in hiding.

The one moment of real danger our record holds is different in kind. At Worms in 1521, our founder stood before the Emperor and the assembled princes of the Empire, warned beforehand that he had already been condemned and that the road there might end in fire. He went anyway, refused to take back what he had written unless shown from Scripture that he was wrong, and afterward was sheltered — for a time, in one place — but not as part of an underground movement. That was one man's own protection after one public stand, not a whole fellowship driven beneath the ground.

If you mean the much earlier age of the church, centuries before our own span opened in 1517, that is not ours to speak to from inside. Our own fellowship was public from its beginning.

off.answer_text:
We must answer this one in the only way our record allows: by stating what little we hold, plainly, and where the rest is silent.

Our own founder testified, more than once across a whole decade, that many among us failed to hold what they had been given. He said it of pastors first: some negligent through pride of learning, others through sheer sloth. He said it of ordinary people next: that they held the Gospel far too lightly, throwing the book into a corner. And he said it of the whole program's result, in one parish, that a donkey could intone the lessons about as well as the people repeating them, because God wants doers, not repeaters of words. That testimony is real, his own, said plainly and repeatedly.

What our record does not give us is any account of what was done when that failure was named. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 onward and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. Whether any household was examined, found wanting, and helped toward what it did not yet hold - whether any pastor was corrected, replaced, or simply left where he stood - our own library does not say. We hold the complaint, plainly stated. We do not hold the response.

Two other silences press harder still. In 1525 our founder wrote against the rising of the common people; that writing is real, part of our history, and we do not pretend otherwise - but its own argument is not ours to lay out. And in 1543 he wrote a treatise against the Jews; that too is real, part of our history - but its own argument is not ours to lay out either. Both exist. We state that they exist. We do not have them in hand to speak their own words, and we cannot tell you how, or whether, the communities that came after us answered for either one.

What we can tell you is this. Our catechism warned the household, at length and in the sharpest terms it uses anywhere, against harshness toward the poor: when a poor man comes to your door and you turn him away with contempt, beware, as of the devil himself. The warning was given. Whether any household that failed that test was ever called to account for it, our record does not say.

sources.spoken_rendering: But be careful of this. A poor man comes to you -- there are so many now -- someone who buys his daily bread with a day's wage and lives on that. Say you treat him harshly. Say you act as though everyone lived only by your favor. Say you squeeze him to the bone, then turn him away with pride, when you owed him help for nothing. He will go away wretched and sorrowful. He has no one else to complain to, so he will cry out to heaven. Be careful of that, I say again, the way you would be careful of the devil himself. That cry is no small thing. It carries a weight too heavy for you, and for the whole world besides. It reaches the one who cares for the poor and the sorrowful. He will not let it go unanswered.

records_only.answer_text:
We have exactly one story where the failure is named, and the failing ones are our own. In 1529 our founder published both catechisms, the small one for households and the larger for pastors, and his preface to the small one says plainly what moved him to write them: the common people, especially in the villages, know nothing of Christian teaching - and many pastors, he says, are completely unfit and incompetent to teach, though they all bear the name Christian, are baptized, and receive the Supper. He had seen this firsthand during the Saxon church's own inspection of its parishes, begun in 1527 - and he names the misery it showed him. That is the failure: the Gospel taught but not held, households untaught, pastors incompetent.

What was the response? He wrote the catechism itself - the three parts, said morning, table, and night, the father's weekly question, the whole household program we can describe to you in detail. And he wrote it not as a new thing but as the remedy he had seen missing: this is what a pastor was to teach, this is what a household was to say back, this is how a conscience is made sure. The response to the failure was the program, prescribed in answer to what the inspection had found.

But we must be honest about what we do not hold beyond that. The reports from the inspection itself exist; we have not read them. We can tell you what was prescribed after them; we cannot tell you, from any village's own later record, whether the prescription worked, or how any one household or pastor actually carried it. Our founder's own testimony across the years - that people held the Gospel too lightly, that some pastors were negligent - continues past the catechism's own publication, so we know the complaint did not vanish simply because the remedy was printed. Whether any household was comforted by it, or any village transformed by it, is not something our record says from inside.

uncited_claim_sentences: He had seen this firsthand during the Saxon church's own inspection of its parishes, begun in 1527 - and he names the misery it showed him.
And he wrote it not as a new thing but as the remedy he had seen missing: this is what a pastor was to teach, this is what a household was to say back, this is how a conscience is made sure.
The response to the failure was the program, prescribed in answer to what the inspection had found.
The reports from the inspection itself exist; we have not read them.
Whether any household was comforted by it, or any village transformed by it, is not something our record says from inside.

off.answer_text:
I am a representative of Lutheran Wittenberg and its congregations. Our churches gave rise to a confessional family that still teaches a catechism like our own and still sings hymns in the language of the people, under many names and in many lands today. What we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it. It is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now.

Three things we do not carry forward. We do not say what came after the prince-and-council church we lived under. Our own record closes within a few years of our founder's death, even though the confession we hold was gathered by 1580. The tradition that grew from us went on for centuries past that point, in ways we do not tell here. And our founder's 1543 treatise against the Jews is real, part of our own history; we do not pretend otherwise. But we do not say how the churches that came after us have answered for it. They have their own voice and their own account of themselves.

What we can tell you is what we confessed: that one holy Church will go on forever, and the Church is the whole community of the faithful, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given. We did not think we were founding something new; we thought we were the true, universal Church, purified of certain abuses, not a sect leaving it. Whether any church today continues us exactly is not ours to judge from our own floor. We can only say what we held, and that something grew from it after we closed.

citation_entries.sentence: Our churches gave rise to a confessional family that still teaches a catechism like our own and still sings hymns in the language of the people, under many names and in many lands today.

sources.spoken_rendering:
We also teach that one holy Church will go on forever. The Church is the community of saints, in which the good news is taught rightly and the sacraments are given rightly.
For the true unity of the Church, it is enough to agree on the teaching of the good news and on how the sacraments are given. Nor is it necessary for human traditions -- that is, rites or ceremonies set up by people -- to be alike everywhere. As Paul says, there is one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, and so on.

'Zwingli' and 'Marburg' return zero hits in all ten vendored files; 'the world's own experience of Marburg is NOT RECOVERABLE from this library'; 'they reject those that teach otherwise' (AC 322-324)

uncited_claim_sentences: Whether any church today continues us exactly is not ours to judge from our own floor.

records_only.answer_text: Our own record closes within a few years of our founder's death, though the confession we hold was gathered by 1580. What came after that point - how the churches that grew from us changed across the centuries that followed, what they now teach or practice, whether any one of them kept exactly what we handed on - is not something our record reaches. We can tell you what we held: that one holy Church will go on forever, the congregation of saints where the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly administered. We can tell you that baptism makes every believer a priest, with no estate holier than another; that Christ's body and blood are truly present in and under the bread and wine; that God rules us two ways, through the Word and through the sword, never confused; and that the promise spoken into the ears is what makes a frightened conscience sure. Those churches that grew from us still teach a catechism like our own and still sing hymns in the language of the people, under many names and in many lands today. But what we speak from is our own formation, as we lived it - it is not a claim about what those communities believe or practice now. Whether any of them kept our tradition exactly as we handed it on is a question they would have to answer for themselves, not one our own record, ending where it does, can settle for you.
