uncited_claim_sentences: Whether any of them kept our tradition exactly as we handed it on is a question they would have to answer for themselves, not one our own record, ending where it does, can settle for you.

off.answer_text:
We held no single rite that made a person one of us, separate from what a household already did - but every person passed through the same formation, beginning at the font and continuing the rest of their life. Here is what we held, in the order it was actually given.

First: baptism, given to children. Water joined to God's command, necessary for salvation, marking a death begun once and renewed every day - the old self drowned, a new self rising. This made every believer a priest already, through baptism itself, before any other thing was done. The child offered to God through baptism was received into his grace on that ground alone, not by any choice the child had yet made.

Second: the household program, taught from the earliest years a child could speak. Every morning the household blessed itself and prayed; every evening the same. Three times a day the three parts were said - the commandments, the creed, the Lord's Prayer - and food was withheld from a child until the words were said back correctly. Once a week, at least, a father sat down with his children and servants and examined them on what they knew, asking the catechism's own question after every part: what does this mean? Not memory only - meaning.

Third: confession, kept as a treasured practice though never compelled. Two parts: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself, without doubting it. We never demanded a full list of every sin; the comfort itself was the point.

Fourth, and only then: the Supper, examined before entry, never forced. None came to it unquestioned - worthiness at the table meant believing the words given for you, not being sinless. A person who could not yet say the three parts was not yet counted among us. But we held the weak inside by patience before we held them inside by full knowledge, and no one was ever driven toward the table by force.

That is the whole formation: font, household catechism, confession, table - examined at every step, comforted at every step, never graduating, saying the same three parts again the next week even after a lifetime under them. One holy Church will go on forever, and the Church is the whole community of the faithful, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given. We did not think we were founding something new; we thought we were the true, universal Church, purified of certain abuses, not a sect leaving it.

What we have just described is the program every household was told to follow, stated plainly in the sources we hold. Whether any one household kept it exactly this way - whether the weekly examination actually happened, whether the daily prayers were actually said - is a question our own record does not answer from the inside. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we have not read them. We hold the instruction, not a village's own report of itself.

uncited_claim_sentences: Here is what we held, in the order it was actually given.
Second: the household program, taught from the earliest years a child could speak.
Fourth, and only then: the Supper, examined before entry, never forced.

That is the whole formation: font, household catechism, confession, table - examined at every step, comforted at every step, never graduating, saying the same three parts again the next week even after a lifetime under them.
What we have just described is the program every household was told to follow, stated plainly in the sources we hold.

records_only.answer_text:
Here is what we can tell you, and what we cannot.

A person becomes one of us the way the confession names us: the community of the faithful, wherever the Gospel is rightly taught and the sacraments rightly given. That membership begins at baptism. We baptize children, and defend it plainly: baptism is necessary for salvation, we say, and through baptism the grace of God is offered. A child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground, not on a choice the child makes for himself. That is the entry. Everything after it is formation.

The household is where that formation happens. A father examines his children and servants at least once a week on the three parts every Christian must know: the Ten Commandments, the Creed, and the Lord's Prayer. Those parts are said daily, at rising, at table, and at night. Food is withheld from a child who will not learn them. After every part, the father asks the catechism's own question: what does this mean? — so a child explains the teaching, not simply repeats it from memory. Confession has two parts as well: admitting sin, then hearing forgiveness spoken as though from God himself. We treasure this practice. We never force it, and we never demand a full list of every sin.

None come to the Supper unquestioned. Before a person approaches that table, they are examined on the three parts. Worthiness at the table means simply believing the words "given for you". The truly unworthy are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all. We examine. We do not compel. No one is driven toward the table by force.

That is the program: baptism first, household formation daily, examination before the Supper, the promise carried to the ears where it can be heard.

What we cannot tell you is whether any one household or parish actually walked through this program exactly as the book prescribes. The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them. We hold the program every household was told to follow, not a single village's own report of itself. We hold our founder's own testimony, given more than once, that people held the Gospel too lightly and that some pastors were negligent — but that is his testimony, not a parish's own record. We can describe the formation mechanism to the hour. Whether it worked the way it was prescribed is not something our own record lets us say from the inside.

sources.locus: 'an ass can almost intone the lessons... God does not want hearers and repeaters of words, but doers and followers' (v2 14676-14688); 'we see to our sorrow that many pastors and preachers are very negligent' (LC 51-52); Katharina von Bora's own question about coldness in prayer (TT 3147-3150)

Luther's own answer to the coldness question, verified verbatim there against cic/texts/luther_table-talk_bell1886.txt lines 3143-3152 -- 'the devil drives on his own servants continually, diligent in their false worship... but we, indeed, are ice cold therein, and negligent'

uncited_claim_sentences: That membership begins at baptism.
A child offered to God through baptism is received into his grace on exactly that ground, not on a choice the child makes for himself.
That is the entry.
Everything after it is formation.
The household is where that formation happens.
Before a person approaches that table, they are examined on the three parts.
The truly unworthy are people who feel no need for forgiveness at all.
No one is driven toward the table by force.
The Saxon church inspected its own parishes from 1527 and wrote down what it found; those reports exist, and we do not hold them.
Whether it worked the way it was prescribed is not something our own record lets us say from the inside.
